title: Gandhi's Gita
hook: a book that opens on a battlefield, read by a man of nonviolence

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gandhi's Gita began with a law student in London who admitted he had never read it, and later learned its verses by the washbasin.

Two armies face each other on an open field. Conch shells sound across the lines. A warrior named Arjuna asks his charioteer to drive out into the gap between them. He looks across and sees teachers, uncles, cousins, old friends. His bow slips from his hand. That's where the Bhagavad Gita begins, weapons about to be loosed. Gandhi, the man the world knew for nonviolence, kept this book close and called it a guide for his life. How does a man of peace live by a book set on a battlefield?
screen: `TWO ARMIES, ONE GAP BETWEEN THEM.` → `ARJUNA'S BOW SLIPS.` → `A MAN OF PEACE, A BOOK OF WAR?`

segments.voice: Gandhi made his own version of the Gita in Gujarati and called it Anasakti Yoga. In its introduction he says that he didn't read the war as history. He read the field as the human heart. The two armies, in his reading, are the forces of good and evil inside one person, and the battle is the one each of us fights there. Krishna, the charioteer, is for him the dweller within, the voice that speaks from the inside. So when Krishna tells Arjuna to stand up and fight, Gandhi hears: don't run from the struggle inside you. A text that seems to send a man into battle becomes, in his hands, a handbook for a nonviolent life. After years of trying to live the Gita's teaching, he wrote, he found its complete selflessness isn't possible without nonviolence. This is one reading among several. Other readers, traditional commentators among them, take the war as a real war and Arjuna's duty as a warrior's real duty: Krishna tells a soldier to do what his role asks, without hatred and without clinging to victory. Still others hold both at once, a real field and a mirror of the inner one. The Gita's first line names the place twice: dharmakshetra, kurukshetra. The field of dharma, the field of the Kurus. Read Gandhi's way, the first name carries the weight: the field of right living is the ground between what a person wants to do and what they know is right.
screen: `HE READ THE FIELD AS THE HEART.` · `KRISHNA: THE DWELLER WITHIN.` · `ONE READING AMONG SEVERAL.` · `THE FIELD OF DHARMA, THE FIELD OF THE KURUS.` · then, large: `THE BATTLE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small battle you're in: something you want to say and suspect you shouldn't, or something you know is right and keep putting off. Do what Arjuna did, and drive out into the gap to look at both sides calmly, the side that pulls on the in-breath, the side that asks on the out-breath, without choosing yet. If you pray, you can hold the whole field before Krishna, or before the one you pray to.
Gandhi's Gita. The Bhagavad Gita as Gandhi read it: a battle fought inside the heart, with Krishna as the voice within.
Your line: the battle is inside. Tomorrow, the one word Gandhi put on the cover. That's day nine hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Readers of Gandhi's Anasakti Yoga often read the Gita's battle as a picture of the struggle within, and some Hindus keep a short daily reading of the Gita alongside their prayers.

chat.says: Gandhi was all about nonviolence. Why would he love a book set on a battlefield?
options: He read the battlefield as the heart, where good and evil fight inside us.
He rewrote the story so that no battle happens at all in his version.
He only read the gentle later verses and skipped the opening chapters.
chat.meaning: In Anasakti Yoga, Gandhi read the field as the human heart, the two armies as good and evil within, and Krishna as the dweller within.

Anasakti Yoga.meaning: Gandhi's Gujarati version of the Gita; anasakti means non-attachment

Arjuna.meaning: the warrior prince whose doubt opens the Gita

dharmakshetra.meaning: the field of dharma, the Gita's first name for the battlefield

kurukshetra.meaning: the field of the Kurus, where the Gita's two armies meet

Krishna.meaning: Arjuna's charioteer and teacher in the Gita, honored as God

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 1:1 and 1:20–47 (the field named; Arjuna between the armies)
Anasakti Yoga, Gandhi's introduction (the battlefield as the heart; Krishna as the dweller within; selflessness and nonviolence)

notes: All Gandhi material is paraphrase: Gandhi's own writings and Mahadev Desai's English rendering are not quoted. Confirm the introduction to Anasakti Yoga says he did not read the Mahabharata/Gita war as history, that the battle is the duel between good and evil in the heart, that Krishna is the 'dweller within', and that he found perfect renunciation impossible without perfect ahimsa ('after years of trying' paraphrases his own count of years, deliberately left unstated).

The other readings (a real war and a warrior's duty; both at once) are described without names or counts. A Keeper may wish to name a commentator (e.g. Tilak or the classical commentators) or leave as is.
